claim: The text mining system achieved F-scores of around 92% for both sex and age when evaluated on 50 randomly selected full-text articles.
source: The F-scores that resulted from this evaluation were around 92% for both sex and age (Table 1), which indicates good quality of the results (Ananiadou et al., 2006).
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental evaluation data presented in Table 1, showing precision, recall, and F-scores for the text mining system, and is compared against established quality standards cited from Ananiadou et al., 2006.

claim: A total of 15,311 full-text articles from the PubMed Central Open Access subset as of February 2015 were processed in this study.
source: A total of 15,311 full-text articles from the PubMed Central Open Access subset as of February 2015 were processed in this study.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the dataset size used in the study.

claim: The corpus of 15,311 documents corresponds to 7.15% of mouse experimentation articles retrieved by the same query in PubMed and 27.85% in PubMed Central.
source: These articles correspond to 7.15% and 27.85% of mouse experimentation articles retrieved by the same query in PubMed and PubMed Central, respectively.
evidence: This claim presents calculated percentages based on the dataset retrieved compared to total available articles.

claim: 50.1% of the corpus articles (n=7,671) were published after 2011.
source: This corpus of documents were published between 1994 and 2014, of which 50.1% were published after 2011 (n= 7,671) (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a statistical summary of the temporal distribution of the corpus, supported by data shown in Figure 1.

claim: PLOS ONE contained the highest number of articles in the corpus (n=5,574; 36.41%).
source: PLOS ONE contained the highest number of articles (n= 5,574; 36.41%), followed by Journal of Experimental Medicine (n= 931; 6.08%), and Journal of Cell Biology (n= 363; 2.37%).
evidence: This presents descriptive statistics about the distribution of articles across journals in the corpus.

claim: About a fifth of papers from 1994 to 2014 did not report either the sex or the age of the mouse used in the study.
source: Overall, from 1994 to 2014, about a fifth of papers did not report either the sex or the age of the mouse used in the study (Figure 1a and 1b).
evidence: This claim summarizes the overall reporting rate across the entire time period, supported by data visualized in Figure 1a and 1b.

claim: The frequency of articles reporting sex and/or age in mice models has increased steadily during the last two decades.
source: Figure 1c shows that the frequency of articles reporting sex and/or age in mice models has increased steadily during the last two decades, whereas missing information about these two experimental variables showed an important drop from 100% (no papers reported the sex and age of the mice in 1994 and 1995) to about 15% following a slope of approximately -0.045.
evidence: This claim describes a temporal trend observed in the data, with specific quantitative details about the rate of change.

claim: Since 2012, the percentage of articles reporting both sex and age had reached only about 50% of the papers published in those years.
source: Nevertheless, since 2012, the percentage of articles reporting both factors had reached only about 50% of the papers published in those years.
evidence: This presents a specific finding about reporting rates in recent years based on the analyzed data.

claim: Experiments performed with female mice were more frequently reported than experiments performed with male mice (31.84% vs. 23.38%, Binomial test p< 0.001; 95% IC: 56.60 – 58.71).
source: When the sex of the mouse model is stated in the article, experiments performed with female mice were more frequently reported than experiments performed with male mice (31.84% vs. 23.38%, Binomial test p< 0.001; 95% IC: 56.60 – 58.71) (Figure 1d).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (binomial test) of the data, with specific percentages and confidence intervals provided.

claim: Female mice have been reported more often than male mice historically, reaching a plateau of about 33% since the last decade (2004-2014).
source: Our results showed that, historically, female mice have been reported more often than male mice, reaching a plateau of about 33% since the last decade (2004 – 2014) (Figure 1e).
evidence: This describes a temporal trend in sex reporting observed in the data analysis.

claim: The use of both sexes in mice experiments stratified by sex showed the lowest improvement over time, with a maximum of about 10% of the articles since 2006.
source: In addition, the use of both sexes in mice experiments stratified by sex showed the lowest improvement over time (Figure 1e); with a maximum of about 10% of the articles since 2006.
evidence: This presents a specific finding about the reporting of both sexes over time based on data analysis.

claim: Reporting of mouse age improved steadily from 1999 to 2006, at which point age is reported more than 50% of the time.
source: Reporting of mouse age improved steadily from 1999 to 2006 (Figure 1f), at which point age is reported more than 50% of the time; since 2010 age reporting has plateaued, with between 65 and 70% of articles each year mentioning the age of mice.
evidence: This describes temporal trends in age reporting based on the analyzed data.

claim: Since 2010, age reporting has plateaued, with between 65 and 70% of articles each year mentioning the age of mice.
source: Reporting of mouse age improved steadily from 1999 to 2006 (Figure 1f), at which point age is reported more than 50% of the time; since 2010 age reporting has plateaued, with between 65 and 70% of articles each year mentioning the age of mice.
evidence: This presents a specific finding about recent age reporting rates based on data analysis.

claim: The reporting of sex and age as experimental variables varies across biomedical fields (p < 0.05).
source: A two-way ANOVA without replication was performed to assess the difference in reporting sex and age for each field. Our results showed statistically significant differences, p < 0.05, indicating that the reporting of these experimental factors varies across biomedical fields (Figure 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis (two-way ANOVA) showing significant differences across fields.

claim: Studies on diabetes showed the highest frequency (68%) of reporting both sex and age of mice.
source: In identifying the sex and age of the mouse, for instance, studies on diabetes showed the highest frequency (68%), whereas studies on cancer showed the lowest frequency (48%) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This presents a specific finding comparing reporting rates across disease categories.

claim: Studies on cancer showed the lowest frequency (48%) of reporting both sex and age of mice.
source: In identifying the sex and age of the mouse, for instance, studies on diabetes showed the highest frequency (68%), whereas studies on cancer showed the lowest frequency (48%) (Figure 2a).
evidence: This presents a specific finding comparing reporting rates across disease categories.

claim: Studies on cancer reported the worst results regarding missing information about sex (33%) or age (37%) of the mice used.
source: Studies on cancer reported the worst results regarding missing information about sex (33%) or age (37%) of the mice used (Figure 2b and 2c).
evidence: This presents specific percentages of missing information for cancer studies based on data analysis.

claim: The best results in reporting sex and age were achieved by studies on neurological disorders.
source: Overall, the best results in reporting sex and age were achieved by the studies on neurological disorders (Figure 2a, 2b and 2c).
evidence: This is a comparative finding based on analysis of reporting rates across disease categories.

claim: There is a preference for studying the immunology of diseases by using female mouse models.
source: Our results suggest that there is a preference for studying the immunology of these diseases by using female mouse models, whereas there is a tendency to use male mouse models for studying their genetic basis (Figure 3a and 3b).
evidence: This is an interpretation of patterns observed in the data analysis across different research approaches.

claim: There is a tendency to use male mouse models for studying the genetic basis of diseases.
source: Our results suggest that there is a preference for studying the immunology of these diseases by using female mouse models, whereas there is a tendency to use male mouse models for studying their genetic basis (Figure 3a and 3b).
evidence: This is an interpretation of patterns observed in the data analysis across different research approaches.

claim: In physiopathology and therapy subgroups, male mice were more frequently studied in models of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and neurological disorders.
source: Both in physiopathology and in therapy subgroups, male mice were more frequently studied in models of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and neurological disorders, and female mice in models of cancer, lung diseases and infectious diseases (Figure 3c and 3d).
evidence: This describes patterns observed in the data analysis for specific disease categories and research approaches.

claim: In physiopathology and therapy subgroups, female mice were more frequently studied in models of cancer, lung diseases and infectious diseases.
source: Both in physiopathology and in therapy subgroups, male mice were more frequently studied in models of cardiovascular diseases, diabetes and neurological disorders, and female mice in models of cancer, lung diseases and infectious diseases (Figure 3c and 3d).
evidence: This describes patterns observed in the data analysis for specific disease categories and research approaches.

claim: No correlation was observed between the reporting of sex or age as experimental variables and the journal impact factor of the 70 journals that covered 30 or more articles of the corpus.
source: No correlation was observed between the reporting of sex or age as experimental variables and the journal impact factor and h-index of the 70 journals that covered 30 or more articles of the corpus (Figure 5).
evidence: This presents the results of correlation analysis between reporting quality and journal metrics.

claim: No correlation was observed between the reporting of sex or age as experimental variables and the h-index of the 70 journals that covered 30 or more articles of the corpus.
source: No correlation was observed between the reporting of sex or age as experimental variables and the journal impact factor and h-index of the 70 journals that covered 30 or more articles of the corpus (Figure 5).
evidence: This presents the results of correlation analysis between reporting quality and journal metrics.

claim: More than 80% of potential therapeutics fail in human clinical trials after being successful in animal models.
source: However, the translation of scientific findings from animal models to humans is far from straightforward, and more than 80% of potential therapeutics fail in human clinical trials after being successful in animal models (Perrin, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Perrin, 2014.

claim: Spending on preclinical research that is not reproducible amounts to $28 billion per year in the United States.
source: It has been estimated that spending on preclinical research that is not reproducible amounts to $28 billion per year in the United States (Freedman et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Freedman et al., 2015.

claim: The sex and age of mice affect morphological, physiological, immunological and behavioral parameters and influence the outcomes of experiments.
source: In experiments using animals, for instance, the sex and age of the mice should be reported because they affect morphological, physiological, immunological and behavioral parameters and, hence, they influence the outcomes of experiments (Diedrich et al., 2007; Wizemann and Pardue, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Diedrich et al., 2007 and Wizemann and Pardue, 2001.

claim: In many animals (including humans), males have shorter lifespans than females.
source: Considering some taxa exceptions, the general conclusion is that in many animals (including humans), males have shorter lifespans than females (Clutton-Brock and Isvaran, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clutton-Brock and Isvaran, 2007.

claim: Sex differences in lifespan depend to a great extent on sexually dimorphic life-history strategies.
source: Furthermore, from an evolutionary standpoint, these sex differences in lifespan depends to a great extent on sexually dimorphic life-history strategies (such as mating systems; Maklakov and Lummaa, 2013), and on genetic architecture, including both the sex chromosomes (Nguyen and Disteche, 2006) and the mitochondrial DNA (Gemmell et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Maklakov and Lummaa, 2013.

claim: Sex differences in lifespan depend on genetic architecture, including both the sex chromosomes and the mitochondrial DNA.
source: Furthermore, from an evolutionary standpoint, these sex differences in lifespan depends to a great extent on sexually dimorphic life-history strategies (such as mating systems; Maklakov and Lummaa, 2013), and on genetic architecture, including both the sex chromosomes (Nguyen and Disteche, 2006) and the mitochondrial DNA (Gemmell et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nguyen and Disteche, 2006 and Gemmell et al., 2004.

claim: Sex and age play key roles in disease phenotypes, modifying their susceptibility, presentation and response to treatment.
source: Regarding preclinical and clinical studies, sex and age play key roles in disease phenotypes, modifying their susceptibility, presentation and response to treatment (Arnold, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Arnold, 2010.

claim: Some pathologies exhibit a clear sexual dimorphism.
source: Some pathologies exhibit a clear sexual dimorphism (Ober et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ober et al., 2008.

claim: The incidence of stroke is higher in men than women during their lifespan.
source: Using stroke as an example, it is known that its incidence is higher in men than women during their lifespan (Mozaffarian et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mozaffarian et al., 2015.

claim: After the age of 60 years and thus post-menopause, women have more severe strokes than men.
source: However, recent evidence suggests that after the age of 60 years and thus post-menopause, women have more severe strokes than men (Dehlendorff et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dehlendorff et al., 2015.

claim: Sex- and age-dependent differences in protein expression profiles were observed in the heart proteome of female and male C57BL/6 mice of two distinct age groups (14 and 100 weeks).
source: In the case of animal models, sex- and age-dependent differences in protein expression profiles were observed in the heart proteome of female and male C57BL/6 mice of two distinct age groups (14 and 100 weeks) (Diedrich et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Diedrich et al., 2007.

claim: Not all papers in journals that endorsed ARRIVE guidelines comply with the ARRIVE guidelines.
source: However, although these guidelines have been endorsed by many journals, not all papers in these journals comply with the ARRIVE guidelines (Baker et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baker et al., 2014.

claim: The mouse is probably the most comprehensive and well-characterized model in the life sciences.
source: We selected the mouse as a model because it is probably the most comprehensive and well-characterized model in the life sciences.
evidence: This is a statement based on general scientific knowledge about the use of mouse models.

claim: About 90% of human genes have direct orthologues with mice.
source: One of the main reasons is that mouse and human genomes are genetically similar – about 90% of human genes have direct orthologues with mice (Yue et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Yue et al., 2014.

claim: Mice have a short lifespan of up to two years.
source: Moreover, as animal models, mice are convenient due to their small size, short lifespan (up to two years), and quick generation time; three weeks for gestation and from 6 to 8 weeks to reach sexual maturity.
evidence: This is a statement based on established biological knowledge about mice.

claim: Mice have a gestation period of three weeks.
source: Moreover, as animal models, mice are convenient due to their small size, short lifespan (up to two years), and quick generation time; three weeks for gestation and from 6 to 8 weeks to reach sexual maturity.
evidence: This is a statement based on established biological knowledge about mice.

claim: Mice reach sexual maturity from 6 to 8 weeks.
source: Moreover, as animal models, mice are convenient due to their small size, short lifespan (up to two years), and quick generation time; three weeks for gestation and from 6 to 8 weeks to reach sexual maturity.
evidence: This is a statement based on established biological knowledge about mice.

claim: The improvement in reporting of sex and age started before the publication of the ARRIVE guidelines in 2010.
source: Whilst an improvement in the reporting of mouse sex and age has been observed over time, this is not solely attributable to the introduction of journal guidelines, because this improvement started before the publication of the ARRIVE guidelines in 2010 (Kilkenny et al., 2010).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the temporal analysis of reporting trends in relation to the publication date of ARRIVE guidelines.

claim: A follow-up study in 2012 showed that journals that enforced the ARRIVE guidelines as a condition of publication still failed to publish sex and age in all cases.
source: In fact, a follow-up study in 2012 showed that while sex and age reporting had improved post-ARRIVE, journals that enforced the ARRIVE guidelines as a condition of publication still failed to publish sex and age in all cases (Baker et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Baker et al., 2014.

claim: The observed improvements in reporting may be a result of a growing recognition of the importance of sex and age as experimental factors that may affect study outcomes.
source: The observed improvements may also therefore be a result of a growing recognition of the importance of sex and age as experimental factors that may affect study outcomes.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for the observed trends in reporting.

claim: Previous studies concluded that males in both human and other animals are studied much more than their female counterparts.
source: An analysis of the scientific literature leads to the general conclusion that the males in both human and other animals are studied much more than their female counterparts. This conclusion is based mainly on the results of two studies that manually surveyed a set of biomedical articles (Beery and Zucker, 2011; Taylor et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim summarizes findings from previous studies cited as Beery and Zucker, 2011 and Taylor et al., 2011.

claim: Female mice are cheaper to house than male mice.
source: This could be explained by some practical advantages of using female rather than male mice: they are cheaper to house; they are less aggressive to each other and to experimenters; and they are smaller, requiring less weight-administered drug.
evidence: This is a statement based on practical knowledge about housing mice.

claim: Female mice are less aggressive to each other and to experimenters than male mice.
source: This could be explained by some practical advantages of using female rather than male mice: they are cheaper to house; they are less aggressive to each other and to experimenters; and they are smaller, requiring less weight-administered drug.
evidence: This is a statement based on practical knowledge about mouse behavior.

claim: Female mice are smaller than male mice, requiring less weight-administered drug.
source: This could be explained by some practical advantages of using female rather than male mice: they are cheaper to house; they are less aggressive to each other and to experimenters; and they are smaller, requiring less weight-administered drug.
evidence: This is a statement based on practical knowledge about mouse physiology.

claim: The strongest male-bias was observed in cardiovascular disease models (2.25:1).
source: Among the main preclinical research topics assessed, we observed the strongest male-bias in cardiovascular disease models (2.25:1) and the strongest female-bias in infectious disease models (3.54:1) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This presents a specific quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The strongest female-bias was found in infectious disease models (3.54:1).
source: Among the main preclinical research topics assessed, we observed the strongest male-bias in cardiovascular disease models (2.25:1) and the strongest female-bias in infectious disease models (3.54:1) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This presents a specific quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: Between 2012 and 2014, about 70% of research articles assessed on cardiovascular disease models are still biased towards male mice.
source: This situation still persists: between 2012 and 2014, about 70% and 77% of research articles assessed on these two disease models are still biased towards male and female mice, respectively.
evidence: This presents a specific finding about recent trends in sex bias for cardiovascular disease models.

claim: Between 2012 and 2014, about 77% of research articles assessed on infectious disease models are still biased towards female mice.
source: This situation still persists: between 2012 and 2014, about 70% and 77% of research articles assessed on these two disease models are still biased towards male and female mice, respectively.
evidence: This presents a specific finding about recent trends in sex bias for infectious disease models.

claim: In the study of hypertension, a greater increase in blood pressure was reported in gonad-intact XY males than XX females using the four core genotype in the MF1 mouse model.
source: For example, in the study of hypertension, one of the major risk factors for cardiovascular disease, a greater increase in blood pressure was reported in gonad-intact XY males than XX females using the four core genotype in the MF1 mouse model. However, the mean arterial pressure was greater in gonadectomized XX mice compared with XY mice regardless of whether the mice were born with testes or with ovaries (Ji et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ji et al., 2010.

claim: The mean arterial pressure was greater in gonadectomized XX mice compared with XY mice regardless of whether the mice were born with testes or with ovaries.
source: For example, in the study of hypertension, one of the major risk factors for cardiovascular disease, a greater increase in blood pressure was reported in gonad-intact XY males than XX females using the four core genotype in the MF1 mouse model. However, the mean arterial pressure was greater in gonadectomized XX mice compared with XY mice regardless of whether the mice were born with testes or with ovaries (Ji et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Ji et al., 2010.

claim: Females have a more robust immune system than males – both the innate and adaptive immune responses.
source: On the other hand, in the case of infectious diseases, females have a more robust immune system than males – both the innate and adaptive immune responses, which makes them less susceptible to developing many infections (mainly Th1-type infections), although it increases the risk of developing autoimmune diseases due to their trend to develop a stronger pro-inflammatory response (Pennell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pennell et al., 2012.

claim: Females are less susceptible to developing many infections (mainly Th1-type infections).
source: On the other hand, in the case of infectious diseases, females have a more robust immune system than males – both the innate and adaptive immune responses, which makes them less susceptible to developing many infections (mainly Th1-type infections), although it increases the risk of developing autoimmune diseases due to their trend to develop a stronger pro-inflammatory response (Pennell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pennell et al., 2012.

claim: Females have an increased risk of developing autoimmune diseases due to their trend to develop a stronger pro-inflammatory response.
source: On the other hand, in the case of infectious diseases, females have a more robust immune system than males – both the innate and adaptive immune responses, which makes them less susceptible to developing many infections (mainly Th1-type infections), although it increases the risk of developing autoimmune diseases due to their trend to develop a stronger pro-inflammatory response (Pennell et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Pennell et al., 2012.

claim: Diabetes disease mouse models were found to be male-biased (1.57:1) from a global point of view.
source: Diabetes disease mouse models exemplified this situation. From a global point of view, this disease was found to be male-biased (1.57:1) (Figure 2b).
evidence: This presents a specific quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: In studies related with the immunology of diabetes, there was a strong female-bias (7.87:1).
source: However, in studies related with the immunology of diabetes, there was a strong female-bias (7.87:1) (Figure 3b); a change that remains in the study of diabetes mellitus type 2 (Figure 4).
evidence: This presents a specific quantitative finding from the data analysis.

claim: The National Institutes of Health (NIH) have proposed a multi-dimensional initiative to balance sex of animals and cells in preclinical studies, which includes extramural training on experimental design and data analysis by sex.
source: In order to balance sex of animals and cells in preclinical studies, the National Institutes of Health (NIH) have proposed a multi-dimensional initiative, which includes, among other things, extramural training on experimental design and data analysis by sex (Clayton and Collins, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Clayton and Collins, 2014.

claim: Text mining can be used to assess reporting of experimental factors in a cost-effective manner.
source: In this context, our study provides an implementation of text mining to assess reporting of experimental factors. By knowing where there is imbalance for a particular variable, it is possible to address it in a cost-effective manner.
evidence: This is an inference about the utility of the text mining approach demonstrated in the study.

claim: Knowing where there is imbalance for a particular variable directly contributes to the comparability of experimental work and to the reproducibility of findings.
source: By knowing where there is imbalance for a particular variable, it is possible to address it in a cost-effective manner. This not only directly contributes to the comparability of experimental work, but also to the reproducibility of findings.
evidence: This is an inference about the implications of identifying reporting imbalances.

claim: Some journals are introducing editorial measures and methods checklists in order to improve the quality of scientific reporting.
source: To address this problem some journals are already introducing editorial measures and methods checklists in order to improve the quality of scientific reporting (Nature, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Nature, 2013.

claim: Journal checklists may make reference to species strain, sex and age of animals, but the main focus is on statistical issues to ensure repeatability, rather than biological factors that modify the outcomes.
source: Nevertheless, whilst journal checklists may make reference to species strain, sex and age of animals, the main focus is on statistical issues to ensure repeatability, rather than biological factors that modify the outcomes.
evidence: This is an observation about the current focus of journal checklists based on the authors' assessment.

claim: The sample does not represent the entire biomedical literature because not all journals are found in the PubMed Central Open Access subset.
source: Whilst this work constitutes the largest analysis of the reporting of sex and age data for mouse-based research to date, our sample does not represent the entire biomedical literature: not all journals are found in the PubMed Central Open Access subset, and some of the journals that deposit their contents into PubMed Central include only some of their articles in the Open Access subset. This is undoubtedly a limitation of our study.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation based on the data source used.

claim: Some journals that deposit their contents into PubMed Central include only some of their articles in the Open Access subset.
source: Whilst this work constitutes the largest analysis of the reporting of sex and age data for mouse-based research to date, our sample does not represent the entire biomedical literature: not all journals are found in the PubMed Central Open Access subset, and some of the journals that deposit their contents into PubMed Central include only some of their articles in the Open Access subset. This is undoubtedly a limitation of our study.
evidence: This is an acknowledgment of a limitation based on the data source used.

claim: This work constitutes the largest analysis of the reporting of sex and age data for mouse-based research to date.
source: Whilst this work constitutes the largest analysis of the reporting of sex and age data for mouse-based research to date, our sample does not represent the entire biomedical literature: not all journals are found in the PubMed Central Open Access subset, and some of the journals that deposit their contents into PubMed Central include only some of their articles in the Open Access subset.
evidence: This is a claim about the scope of the current study relative to previous work.

claim: The reason why sex and age variables are not described is unclear.
source: The reason why these variables are not described is unclear, since this simple information is always available to researchers.
evidence: This is an observation about the lack of clear explanation for non-reporting.

claim: It is possible to describe sex, age, mice number and mouse strain in about 40 characters of text.
source: We do not believe it is a space issue, because it is possible to describe them, including mice number and mouse strain, in about 40 characters of text (e.g. ten C57BL/6 female mice (6-8-weeks old)).
evidence: This is a demonstration based on an example provided.

claim: The apparent contradiction between the finding that female mice are reported more often and previous reports of male bias might be related to the sample size and study design.
source: In addition, the apparent contradiction between this observation and the previous reports might be related to the sample size and study design; our sample size was larger and we surveyed a much broader range of disciplines.
evidence: This is a speculative explanation for differences between current and previous findings.

claim: Previous studies on sex bias included other species such as cat, dog and monkey models, not just rodent models.
source: In addition, although rodent models (that is, mouse and rat models) accounted for, respectively, 50% and 80% of the papers considered in these other studies (Beery and Zucker, 2011; Taylor et al., 2011), they also included other species, such as cat, dog and monkey models: moreover, these two studies did not explore sex bias by species.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology of previous studies cited.

claim: Previous studies did not explore sex bias by species.
source: In addition, although rodent models (that is, mouse and rat models) accounted for, respectively, 50% and 80% of the papers considered in these other studies (Beery and Zucker, 2011; Taylor et al., 2011), they also included other species, such as cat, dog and monkey models: moreover, these two studies did not explore sex bias by species.
evidence: This is a description of the methodology of previous studies cited.

claim: Cardiovascular diseases, cancer, diabetes mellitus, lung diseases, infectious diseases, and neurological disorders are among the top 10 causes of death according to the W.H.O.
source: In order to identify whether there are general features common on reporting sex and age as experimental variables to any biomedical field, we assessed six main preclinical research topics as defined by their impact on human health (WHO, 2014), including: cardiovascular diseases; cancer; diabetes mellitus; lung diseases; infectious diseases; and neurological disorders.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2014.

claim: Melanoma is a highly aggressive and notoriously chemoresistant form of cancer, making it a widely used tumor model.
source: Melanoma was included for the cancer group since it is a highly aggressive and notoriously chemoresistant form of cancer; making it a widely used tumor model (Herlyn and Fukunaga-Kalabis, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Herlyn and Fukunaga-Kalabis, 2010.

claim: In most specific disease cases, there is a similar pattern of reporting as that found for the biomedical fields assessed to which these diseases belong.
source: Overall, our results suggest that in most cases there is a similar pattern of reporting as that found for the biomedical fields assessed to which these diseases belong (Figure 4).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from comparing specific disease reporting patterns to broader field patterns.

claim: The number of crafted rules was 12 for sex and 18 for age.
source: The number of crafted rules was 12 for sex and 18 for age.
evidence: This is a description of the text mining methodology used.

claim: It is highly unlikely for researchers to report key information about animal models that they did not use.
source: Since our method focuses on the recognition of age and sex at the mention level per document, we hypothesize that it is highly unlikely for researchers to report key information about animal models that they did not use.
evidence: This is a hypothesis underlying the text mining approach.

claim: Through manual inspection of 40 randomly selected articles, if there are mentions in text (particularly in the Method section) of specific age and sex (together) these are attributed to the mice used in the animal experiments and no further mentions were reported.
source: In order to further support this hypothesis, 40 full-text articles were randomly selected from our corpus and through manual inspection, we concluded that indeed, if there are mentions in text (particularly in the Method section) of specific age and sex (together) these are attributed to the mice used in the animal experiments and no further mentions were reported (Supplementary file 2B).
evidence: This is a finding from manual validation of the text mining approach.

claim: There was no disagreement between the manual annotations performed by two biomedical experts.
source: In order to create an evaluation dataset, 50 full-text articles were randomly selected from our corpus of study (Supplementary file 3D) and were manually double-annotated for both the age and the sex by the first and fourth authors due to their biomedical expertise. There was no disagreement between the manual annotations performed by two biomedical experts.
evidence: This describes the inter-annotator agreement in the evaluation process.

claim: False-negative results regarding age mentions occurred because the rules are based on syntactical patterns that require a numeric range between specific time units.
source: False-negative results regarding age mentions occurred because the rules are based on syntactical patterns that require a numeric range between specific time units, i.e., days, weeks and months.
evidence: This is an explanation for a limitation of the text mining system based on its design.

claim: False-negative results regarding sex mentions occurred because the rules for sex recognition do not enable the identification of sex through inference, such as when sex-specific proxy elements like pregnancy are mentioned.
source: False-negative results regarding sex mentions occurred because the rules for the sex recognition is rather straightforward with a simple dictionary matching (minimal), which, as a consequence, does not enable the identification of the sex through inference, e.g. when sex-specific proxy elements are mentioned, such as pregnancy.
evidence: This is an explanation for a limitation of the text mining system based on its design.

claim: The F-measure of 92% gives enough confidence in using this automated method to assess the incidence of reporting sex and age in biomedical articles.
source: Nevertheless, the F-measure of 92% (Table 1) gives enough confidence in using this automated method to assess the incidence of reporting sex and age in biomedical articles.
evidence: This is an assessment of the reliability of the text mining method based on its performance metrics.

claim: Seventy journals out of the 628 analyzed covered 30 or more articles of the corpus, which corresponds to 81.05% of papers retrieved.
source: Seventy journals out of the 628 analyzed covered 30 or more articles of the corpus (Figure 1—figure supplement 1), which corresponds to 81.05% of papers retrieved.
evidence: This presents descriptive statistics about the distribution of articles across journals.
